newsitem.title: INDIA: India ruling coalition heals policy differences.
newsitem.headline: India ruling coalition heals policy differences.

text.p: India's ruling United Front coalition put on a brave face on Wednesday, saying it had ironed out differences among its members over economic policies.

"We are satisfied with the discussions and the decisions taken," Harkishen Singh Surjeet, general secretary of Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), told reporters after a four-hour meeting of the United Front's policy-making steering panel.
The meeting was held against a backdrop of rising tension between free traders and communists in Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ruling United Front coalition.
The CPI-M is a part of Deve Gowda's coalition but holds no office in the government.
Deve Gowda, along with Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, Industry Minister Murasoli Maran and state chiefs of parties in the United Front coalition attended the meeting.
Chidambaram, who is spearheading the government's economic reform programme, on Tuesday lashed out at Deve Gowda's communist supporters for criticising economic reforms.
"One cannot be in the government and criticise it," the Press Trust of India quoted Chidambaram as saying.

Surjeet, briefing reporters at Deve Gowda's residence, said the coalition members had decided to fulfill the pledges made in a policy blueprint announced in June after the United Front formed the government.
"It was decided to highlight the importance of public sector and the necessity for revival wherever possible," he said.
The steering panel also decided to ask the federal government to supply rice and wheat to people below the poverty line at half of the subsidised rate offered by the government.
"The government has been asked to implement the scheme without delay," Surjeet said.
About 35 percent of India's 920 million population live below the poverty line, mostly in rural areas.
Earlier on Wednesday, the right-wing Hindu opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) had forced the abrupt adjournment of the upper house of parliament.

Vice President Kocheril Raman Narayanan adjourned the Rajya Sabha, or upper house, amid an uproar over populous Uttar Pradesh state, where for weeks the nation's three major political groupings have been fruitlessly jockeying for power.
The lower house, or Lok Sabha, was also quickly adjourned to mourn a deceased member.
The month-long session was expected to test the strength of Deve Gowda's government in the face of the opposition BJP.
The BJP wasted no time raising a complaint over the logjammed political situation in Uttar Pradesh, the nation's most populous state with 140 million people.
The BJP emerged as the biggest single party in recent state assembly elections but short of an outright majority.
The United Front coalition came in second, and the Congress party, allied with a regional party representing the lowest Hindu castes, came in third.

Congress, which provides make-or-break support to Deve Gowda's coalition in the federal parliament but has not joined the government, had demanded that the United Front support its candidate to become Uttar Pradesh chief minister.

But the United Front declined, stoking tension with Congress. Then last month, President Shankar Dayal Sharma imposed federal rule over the state after the sparing parties were unable to form a local government.
